Book: Simon 7.3.1(2) (cone: η_{0,λ#}C = C) and Ch. 6, 2.23 (chapter-06.txt line 408: f_#T(ω) = T(f^#ω)); the cone property is used in the proof of 7.4.5 (chapter-07.txt lines 697–698).

Fix λ > 0 and ω ∈ TestFormOn univ n. Put L := dilationCLM P λ = λ^{-1} · id (a continuous linear map of ℝ^P) and b := −(λ^{-1} · 0), so that dilation 0 λ y = b + L y for all y (definition of dilation), and put V := dilation 0 λ '' univ, the domain of blowUp C 0 λ.

1. IsConeCurrent C, applied to λ, the proof of 0 < λ, and ω, gives currentEval (blowUp C 0 λ) ω = C(ω).

2. V = ℝ^P: every x ∈ ℝ^P equals dilation 0 λ (λx), because −(λ^{-1}·0) + λ^{-1}(λx) = 0 + x = x (λ ≠ 0). Hence tsupport ω ⊆ V. Moreover ω is a test form (smooth with compact support; first component of ω.property). So the condition h : IsTestForm ω ∧ tsupport ω ⊆ V in the definition of currentEval holds, the 'if' takes its positive branch, and currentEval (blowUp C 0 λ) ω = (blowUp C 0 λ) ⟨ω, h⟩.

By the contract's definition, blowUp C 0 λ = (C.restrictDomain h_sub).affinePushforward L b h_proper, where h_sub is the inclusion (y ↦ b + L y)^{-1}(V) ⊆ univ and h_proper the properness of y ↦ b + Ly (both proved inside the definition of blowUp). By GeometricCurrentOn.affinePushforward_apply and GeometricCurrentOn.restrictDomain_apply (both hold by rfl),
 (blowUp C 0 λ) ⟨ω, h⟩ = C(ω'), where ω' := testFormOnInclusion h_sub n (affinePullbackTestOn L b h_proper V n ⟨ω, h⟩).
 Here ω' is an element of TestFormOn univ n (the SimonGMT constructions affinePullbackTestOn and testFormOnInclusion produce test forms; properness of the affine map is what makes the pulled-back form compactly supported), and its underlying form is (testFormOnInclusion_coe, affinePullbackTestOn_coe, definition of affinePullbackForm)
 ω'(y) = affinePullbackForm L b ω y = (ω(b + L y)).compContinuousLinearMap L for every y ∈ ℝ^P.

4. Combining steps 1–3: C(ω') = (blowUp C 0 λ)⟨ω, h⟩ = currentEval (blowUp C 0 λ) ω = C(ω).

5. Pointwise formula. For every y, b + L y = −(λ^{-1}·0) + λ^{-1}y = λ^{-1}y. Let α := ω(λ^{-1}y), an n-covector, i.e. a continuous alternating n-linear map (ℝ^P)^n → ℝ. For v = (v_1, …, v_n) ∈ (ℝ^P)^n,
 (α.compContinuousLinearMap L)(v) = α(λ^{-1}v_1, …, λ^{-1}v_n) = (∏_{i ∈ Fin n} λ^{-1}) · α(v) = (λ^{-1})^n · α(v),

By extensionality in v, α.compContinuousLinearMap L = (λ^{-1})^n • α. Hence ω'(y) = (λ^{-1})^n • ω(λ^{-1} • y) for every y ∈ ℝ^P.

6. By steps 3–5, ω' ∈ TestFormOn univ n satisfies ω'(y) = (λ^{-1})^n • ω(λ^{-1} • y) for all y and C(ω') = C(ω), which is the claim.

subproblems.title: The tangent space of an embedded submanifold is the range of the derivative of any local representation
subproblems.statement: Let ψ : ℝ^d → ℝ^P be a local representation of N ⊆ ℝ^P in the sense of Simon Ch. 2 §4 (4.1): V ⊆ ℝ^d and W ⊆ ℝ^P open, ψ of class C^r on V with r ≥ 1, ψ injective on V, ψ(V) = W ∩ N, V ∩ ψ^{-1}(K) compact for every compact K ⊆ W, and Dψ(z) injective for every z ∈ V. Then for every v ∈ V the tangent space T_{ψ(v)}N = {γ'(0) : γ ∈ C¹((−1,1); ℝ^P), γ((−1,1)) ⊆ N, γ(0) = ψ(v)} (tangentSpace N (ψ v)) equals the range of Dψ(v).

Source: Simon Ch. 2 §4 (definition of T_yM for an embedded submanifold, and its identification with Dψ(ℝ^d)); used in steps 3 and 6 of the parent proof.
1. Setup. Put y := ψ(v) ∈ W ∩ N and L := Dψ(v) = fderiv ℝ ψ v; since V is open and r ≥ 1, ψ is differentiable at v with derivative L. L is injective, so (finite dimension) there is c > 0 with |Lh| ≥ c|h| for all h ∈ ℝ^d; range L is a linear subspace, hence closed.
2. range L ⊆ T_yN. Let w = La. If a = 0, the constant curve γ ≡ y works (y ∈ N). Otherwise choose ρ > 0 with closedBall(v, ρ) ⊆ V and κ > 0 with κ|a| < ρ, and let σ(s) := κ·tanh(s/κ), a smooth function with σ(0) = 0, σ'(0) = 1 and |σ(s)| < κ. Put γ(s) := ψ(v + σ(s)a). Then v + σ(s)a ∈ V for all s, so γ is C^r (in particular C¹) on ℝ ⊇ (−1,1), γ(ℝ) ⊆ ψ(V) ⊆ N, γ(0) = y, and γ'(0) = Dψ(v)(σ'(0)a) = La = w. Hence w ∈ T_yN.
3. Embedding property. If z_k ∈ V and ψ(z_k) → y then z_k → v: the set K := {ψ(z_k) : k} ∪ {y} is compact and contained in W, so V ∩ ψ^{-1}(K) is compact and contains every z_k; any cluster point z ∈ V of (z_k) satisfies ψ(z) = y = ψ(v) by continuity, so z = v by injectivity on V; hence z_k → v.
4. T_yN ⊆ range L. Let w ∈ T_yN, witnessed by γ. As γ is continuous at 0 and W is open, there is s_0 ∈ (0,1) with γ(s) ∈ W ∩ N = ψ(V) for |s| < s_0; write γ(s) = ψ(β(s)) with β(s) ∈ V (unique by injectivity). By step 3 (applied along sequences s_k → 0), β(s) → v as s → 0.
5. Write ψ(z) − y = L(z − v) + ρ(z) with |ρ(z)| ≤ η(|z − v|)·|z − v|, η(t) → 0 as t → 0. For |s| small, η(|β(s) − v|) ≤ c/2, hence |γ(s) − y| ≥ c|β(s) − v| − (c/2)|β(s) − v|, i.e. |β(s) − v| ≤ (2/c)|γ(s) − y|. Since γ is differentiable at 0, |γ(s) − y| ≤ C|s| for small |s|; thus |β(s) − v| = O(|s|) and |ρ(β(s))| = o(|s|).
6. Hence (γ(s) − y)/s = L((β(s) − v)/s) + o(1), so the difference quotients lie within o(1) of range L. Letting s → 0, w = γ'(0) belongs to the closure of range L, which is range L. Together with step 2, tangentSpace N (ψ v) = Set.range (fderiv ℝ ψ v).

Injectivity of Dψ(v) gives |β(s) − v| = O(|γ(s) − ψ(v)|), so difference quotients of any curve in N lie in range Dψ(v) up to o(1).

Source: step 1 of the parent proof (Simon Ch. 6, §1: coordinate covectors dx^I and the pairing of Λⁿ with Λₙ). The Cauchy–Binet identity is proved inline.
Notation:
- e_0, …, e_{P−1} is the standard basis of ℝ^P (EuclideanSpace.basisFun), and v(i) is the i-th coordinate of v ∈ ℝ^P.
- Λⁿ := Covector (Euclid P) n, the continuous alternating n-linear maps (ℝ^P)^n → ℝ; Λₙ := MultiVector P n = Λⁿ →L[ℝ] ℝ.
- 𝓘 is the finite set of strictly increasing I : Fin n → Fin P, and e_I := (e_{I(0)}, …, e_{I(n−1)}).
- For α ∈ Λⁿ, |α| := covectorEuclideanNorm α = (Σ_{I ∈ 𝓘} α(e_I)²)^{1/2}. The defining sum runs over all I : Fin n → Fin P, with term α(e_I)² for strictly increasing I and 0 otherwise, so it is the same sum.
- For v = (v_0, …, v_{n−1}) ∈ (ℝ^P)^n and I ∈ 𝓘, v^I is the n×n matrix with (k, j) entry v_j(I(k)).
1. (Coordinate covectors.) For I ∈ 𝓘 let dx^I ∈ Λⁿ be dx^I(v) := det(v^I). It is n-linear and alternating in v, because the determinant is multilinear and alternating in its columns and column j, (v_j(I(k)))_k, depends linearly on v_j. It is continuous because ℝ^P is finite-dimensional. In SimonGMT (Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter06.FormsDuality), dx^I = wedgeCovectors n (fun k ↦ EuclideanSpace.proj (I k)), and wedgeCovectors_apply_det gives exactly this formula. For n = 0, dx^I is the constant covector 1, the determinant of the empty matrix.
2. (Kronecker property.) For I, J ∈ 𝓘, dx^I(e_J) = 1 if I = J and dx^I(e_J) = 0 if I ≠ J. The matrix (e_J)^I has (k, j) entry 1 if I(k) = J(j) and 0 otherwise. If I = J it is the identity matrix. If I ≠ J, the ranges differ, because a strictly increasing map Fin n → Fin P is the increasing enumeration of its range. Both ranges have n elements, so some I(k) is not in range J. Row k of (e_J)^I is then zero, and the determinant is 0.
3. (Expansion.) For every α ∈ Λⁿ and v ∈ (ℝ^P)^n: α(v) = Σ_{I ∈ 𝓘} α(e_I)·dx^I(v).
 Both sides are alternating n-linear functions of v; the right side is a linear combination of the dx^I. By multilinearity, two n-linear maps on ℝ^P agree once they agree on every basis tuple e_f := (e_{f(0)}, …, e_{f(n−1)}), f : Fin n → Fin P.
 - If f is not injective, both alternating maps vanish at e_f, which has a repeated entry.
 - If f is injective, let J ∈ 𝓘 enumerate range f increasingly, and let σ be the permutation of Fin n with f = J ∘ σ. By alternation, each side at e_f equals sign(σ) times its value at e_J. At e_J the right side is Σ_I α(e_I) dx^I(e_J) = α(e_J) by step 2.
 Hence the two sides agree.
4. (Sum of squared minors; Cauchy–Binet.) For every orthonormal family τ = (τ_0, …, τ_{n−1}) in ℝ^P, Σ_{I ∈ 𝓘} det(τ^I)² = 1. This is the Cauchy–Binet formula det(AᵀA) = Σ_I det(A_I)² for the P×n matrix A with columns τ_j, where AᵀA = Id. Self-contained derivation:
 - Let δ_τ ∈ Λⁿ be δ_τ(v) := det(⟨τ_i, v_j⟩)_{i,j}. It is n-linear, alternating and continuous for the same reasons as dx^I, and equals wedgeCovectors n (fun i ↦ ⟨τ_i, ·⟩).
 - By orthonormality, δ_τ(τ) = det(⟨τ_i, τ_j⟩) = det(Id) = 1.
 - δ_τ(e_I) = det(τ_i(I(j)))_{i,j} = det((τ^I)ᵀ) = det(τ^I), and dx^I(τ) = det(τ^I).
 - Step 3 with α = δ_τ and v = τ gives 1 = δ_τ(τ) = Σ_I δ_τ(e_I)·dx^I(τ) = Σ_I det(τ^I)².
5. (Proof of (a).) Let ξ, Q satisfy IsUnitOrientationOf ξ Q, with orthonormal τ and sign s, so ξ(α) = s·α(τ) for all α. For α ∈ Λⁿ, step 3 and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in ℝ^𝓘 give
 |ξ(α)| = |α(τ)| = |Σ_I α(e_I) det(τ^I)| ≤ (Σ_I α(e_I)²)^{1/2}·(Σ_I det(τ^I)²)^{1/2} = |α|·1,
 using step 4.
6. (Definition of L.) For ζ ∈ Λₙ put L(ζ) := Σ_{I ∈ 𝓘} ζ(dx^I)·dx^I. Each ζ ↦ ζ(dx^I) is evaluation at a fixed point, a continuous linear functional on Λₙ. So L is a finite sum of continuous linear maps Λₙ → Λⁿ, i.e. L ∈ (MultiVector P n →L[ℝ] Covector (Euclid P) n). For example, L = Σ_I (ContinuousLinearMap.apply ℝ ℝ (dx^I)).smulRight (dx^I). L does not depend on ξ.
7. (Coefficients of L(ζ).) For J ∈ 𝓘, step 2 gives L(ζ)(e_J) = Σ_I ζ(dx^I)·dx^I(e_J) = ζ(dx^J). Hence |L(ζ)|² = Σ_{J ∈ 𝓘} ζ(dx^J)².
8. (Proof of (b) and (c).) For ξ as in step 5, ξ(dx^J) = s·dx^J(τ) = s·det(τ^J).
 - By step 7 and step 4, |L(ξ)|² = Σ_J s²·det(τ^J)² = 1, so |L(ξ)| = 1 ≤ 1.
 - By linearity of ξ, ξ(L(ξ)) = Σ_I ξ(dx^I)·ξ(dx^I) = Σ_I det(τ^I)² = 1.
9. (Degenerate cases need no separate treatment.)
 - For n = 0, 𝓘 consists of the empty map, e_∅ is the empty tuple, dx^∅ = 1 and |α| = |α(e_∅)|. Steps 1–8 hold verbatim.
 - If n > P, then 𝓘 = ∅ and step 4 would give 0 = 1. So ℝ^P has no orthonormal family of n vectors, the hypothesis IsUnitOrientationOf ξ Q never holds, and the statement is vacuous (L = 0).
proof_key_steps: Define dx^I(v) = det(v_j(I(k)))_{k,j} (SimonGMT wedgeCovectors of coordinate projections); dx^I(e_J) = δ_IJ for strictly increasing I, J.
Expansion α(v) = Σ_I α(e_I)·dx^I(v): both sides are alternating multilinear and agree on all basis tuples.
Σ_I det(τ^I)² = 1 for orthonormal τ (Cauchy–Binet), by expanding δ_τ(v) = det(⟨τ_i, v_j⟩) at v = τ.
Cauchy–Schwarz gives |ξ(α)| = |α(τ)| ≤ |α|.
L(ζ) = Σ_I ζ(dx^I)·dx^I is continuous linear, with |L(ξ)|² = Σ_I det(τ^I)² = 1 and ξ(L(ξ)) = Σ_I det(τ^I)² = 1.

subproblems.title: Two unit orientations of the same n-plane differ by a sign
subproblems.statement: Let P, n ∈ ℕ, let Q be a linear subspace of ℝ^P and let v, w ∈ Λ_n(ℝ^P) (MultiVector P n: continuous linear functionals on n-covectors, ⟨α, v⟩ = v(α)). If v and w are both unit orientations of Q (IsUnitOrientationOf v Q and IsUnitOrientationOf w Q: for some orthonormal families τ, τ' : Fin n → ℝ^P spanning Q, v(α) = ±α(τ) and w(α) = ±α(τ') for all n-covectors α), then w = v or w = −v.

Source: the linear-algebra part of step 3 of the parent proof (orthonormal bases of Q differ by an orthogonal matrix of determinant ±1).

1. Unfolding the hypotheses: there are orthonormal families τ, τ' : Fin n → ℝ^P with span(range τ) = Q = span(range τ'), and signs ε, ε' ∈ {1, −1} with v(α) = ε·α(τ) and w(α) = ε'·α(τ') for every n-covector α (continuous alternating n-linear map ℝ^P → ℝ).

2. Each τ_i and τ'_i lies in Q, so τ, τ' may be regarded as families in the inner product space Q, where they are still orthonormal. Since τ is linearly independent and spans Q, dim Q = n; an orthonormal (hence linearly independent) family of n vectors in the n-dimensional space Q spans Q. Hence τ and τ' are orthonormal bases b and b' of Q indexed by Fin n.

3. Let d := det_b(b'), the determinant of the change-of-basis matrix from b to b'. Both bases are orthonormal, so this matrix is orthogonal and d ∈ {1, −1} (Mathlib OrthonormalBasis.det_to_matrix_orthonormalBasis_real).

4. Let α be an n-covector and α_Q its restriction to Q (α composed with the inclusion Q → ℝ^P in each slot), an alternating n-linear form on the n-dimensional space Q. Every such form is a multiple of det_b: α_Q = α_Q(b)·det_b (Mathlib AlternatingMap.eq_smul_basis_det). Evaluating at b' gives α(τ') = α_Q(b') = α_Q(b)·det_b(b') = d·α(τ). The number d does not depend on α.

5. Hence for every α: w(α) = ε'·α(τ') = ε'd·α(τ) = (εε'd)·(ε·α(τ)) = s·v(α), where s := εε'd ∈ {1, −1} (using ε² = 1). Therefore w = s·v, i.e. w = v if s = 1 and w = −v if s = −1. For n = 0 the same argument applies (τ = τ' is the empty family, Q = {0}, d = 1). ∎
proof_key_steps: Both orthonormal families spanning Q are orthonormal bases b, b' of Q.
det_b(b') = ±1 because the change-of-basis matrix is orthogonal.
For every n-covector α, α(τ') = det_b(b')·α(τ) since alternating n-forms on Q are multiples of det_b.
Therefore w = (εε'det_b(b'))·v with εε'det_b(b') ∈ {±1}.

1. (Two-sided bounds for a fixed ε ∈ (0, 1).) By the sibling lemma near_isometric_chart, choose χ : ℝ^n → ℝ^P and δ, δ' > 0 such that:
 - χ(0) = z;
 - (1 − ε)|a − b| ≤ |χ(a) − χ(b)| ≤ (1 + ε)|a − b| for all a, b ∈ B_δ(0);
 - χ(B_δ(0)) ⊆ M;
 - M ∩ B_{δ'}(z) ⊆ χ(B_δ(0)).
 Let 0 < s < min(δ', (1 − ε)δ), and put r₁ := s/(1 + ε) and r₂ := s/(1 − ε). Then 0 < r₁ ≤ r₂ < δ.
 (a) χ(B_{r₁}(0)) ⊆ M ∩ B_s(z). For |w| < r₁ we have χ(w) ∈ M and |χ(w) − z| = |χ(w) − χ(0)| ≤ (1 + ε)|w| < (1 + ε)r₁ = s.
 (b) M ∩ B_s(z) ⊆ χ(B_{r₂}(0)). Let x ∈ M ∩ B_s(z). Then x ∈ M ∩ B_{δ'}(z), so x = χ(w) with |w| < δ. Hence (1 − ε)|w| ≤ |χ(w) − χ(0)| = |x − z| < s, that is, |w| < r₂.
 (c) Apply the sibling lemma bilipschitz_measure with c₁ = 1 − ε and c₂ = 1 + ε, to E = B_{r₁}(0) and to E = B_{r₂}(0). Both are subsets of B_δ(0), where the bi-Lipschitz bounds hold. With (a), (b) and monotonicity of Hⁿ:
 Hⁿ(M ∩ B_s(z)) ≥ Hⁿ(χ(B_{r₁}(0))) ≥ (1 − ε)ⁿ r₁ⁿ ω_n = ((1 − ε)/(1 + ε))ⁿ sⁿ ω_n,
 Hⁿ(M ∩ B_s(z)) ≤ Hⁿ(χ(B_{r₂}(0))) ≤ (1 + ε)ⁿ r₂ⁿ ω_n = ((1 + ε)/(1 − ε))ⁿ sⁿ ω_n.

2. (Limit.) The real functions ε ↦ ((1 − ε)/(1 + ε))ⁿ and ε ↦ ((1 + ε)/(1 − ε))ⁿ are continuous at 0 with value 1, so their images under ofReal tend to 1 as ε → 0.
 - Given a < 1, choose ε ∈ (0, 1) with ofReal(((1 − ε)/(1 + ε))ⁿ) > a. By step 1, a < R(s) for all sufficiently small s > 0.
 - Given b > 1, choose ε ∈ (0, 1) with ofReal(((1 + ε)/(1 − ε))ⁿ) < b. By step 1, R(s) < b for all sufficiently small s > 0.
 Hence R(s) → 1 as s ↓ 0 (order characterization of convergence in [0, ∞], tendsto_order).

1. (t·Z(C) ⊆ Z(C) for every t > 0.) Let t > 0 and z ∈ Z(C). Choose W ∈ 𝒲 with z ∈ W. Since tz ∈ tW, it suffices to show tW ∈ 𝒲.
 (a) tW is open, because y ↦ ty is a homeomorphism of ℝ^P (t ≠ 0).
 (b) closure(tW) = t·closure(W) by the same homeomorphism. It is compact, as the continuous image of the compact set closure W, and it lies in ℝ^P.
 (c) C vanishes on tW. Let ω ∈ 𝒟ⁿ(ℝ^P) with tsupport ω ⊆ tW. Apply cone_pullback_identity with λ := t⁻¹ > 0. It gives ω' ∈ 𝒟ⁿ(ℝ^P) with C(ω') = C(ω) and ω'(y) = (λ⁻¹)ⁿ ω(λ⁻¹y) = tⁿ ω(ty) for all y.

Terminology. A chart of N at y is a triple (V, W, ψ) as in IsEmbeddedSubmanifold r d N:
- V ⊆ ℝ^d and W ⊆ ℝ^P are open, with y ∈ W;
- ψ is C^r and injective on V, with ψ(V) = W ∩ N;
- V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) is compact for every compact K ⊆ W;
- Dψ(z) is injective for every z ∈ V.

1. (M is an embedded submanifold.) Let y ∈ M. Choose an open O ∋ y as in the hypothesis and a chart (V, W, ψ) of M ∩ O at y (y ∈ M ∩ O). Then (V, W ∩ O, ψ) is a chart of M at y:
 - V is open, W ∩ O is open, and y ∈ W ∩ O;
 - ψ is C^r and injective on V, and Dψ(z) is injective for z ∈ V, unchanged;
 - ψ(V) = W ∩ (M ∩ O) = (W ∩ O) ∩ M;
 - every compact K ⊆ W ∩ O satisfies K ⊆ W, so V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) is compact.
 Hence IsEmbeddedSubmanifold r d M.
2. (Open pieces are submanifolds.) Let O ⊆ ℝ^P be open and w ∈ M ∩ O. By step 1 choose a chart (V, W, ψ) of M at w. As w ∈ W ∩ M = ψ(V), there is v ∈ V with ψ(v) = w. Put V' := V ∩ ψ⁻¹(O) and W' := W ∩ O. Then (V', W', ψ) is a chart of M ∩ O at w:
 - V' is open, since ψ is continuous on the open set V (C^r implies continuous) and O is open. W' is open and w ∈ W'.
 - ψ is C^r and injective on V' ⊆ V, and Dψ(z) is injective for z ∈ V'.
 - ψ(V') = ψ(V) ∩ O = (W ∩ M) ∩ O = W' ∩ (M ∩ O).
 - For compact K ⊆ W' we have ψ⁻¹(K) ⊆ ψ⁻¹(O), so V' ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) = V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K). This is compact because K ⊆ W.
 Moreover v ∈ V', because ψ(v) = w ∈ O. Every w ∈ M ∩ O has such a chart, so IsEmbeddedSubmanifold r d (M ∩ O).
3. (Tangent spaces.) Keep w, v, (V, W, ψ) and (V', W', ψ) from step 2, and use r ≥ 1.
 - chart_tangent_space for N := M and the chart (V, W, ψ) gives tangentSpace M (ψ v) = range Dψ(v).
 - chart_tangent_space for N := M ∩ O and the chart (V', W', ψ) gives tangentSpace (M ∩ O) (ψ v) = range Dψ(v).
 Since ψ(v) = w, tangentSpace (M ∩ O) w = tangentSpace M w. ∎

- H^m := μHE[m], B_s(w) := ball w s, and B_y := B_{ρ(y)}(y).

2. (Positivity, F3.) Let w ∈ M and s > 0. Then H^m(M ∩ B_s(w)) ≠ 0. Otherwise H^m(M ∩ B_{s'}(w)) ≤ H^m(M ∩ B_s(w)) = 0 for 0 < s' < s. So the ratio H^m(M ∩ B_{s'}(w))/(ω_m s'^m) is 0 on (0, s) and tends to 0 as s' ↓ 0. By submanifold_density_one it tends to 1. Limits in [0, ∞] are unique, a contradiction.
3. (Agreement on overlaps.) Let y, y' ∈ M and w ∈ M ∩ B_y ∩ B_{y'}. We show ξ_{y'}(w) = ξ_y(w).
 (a) By the orientation hypotheses there are subspaces Q and Q' such that:
  - Q has carrier tangentSpace(M ∩ B_y, w), and ξ_y(w) is a unit orientation of Q;
  - Q' has carrier tangentSpace(M ∩ B_{y'}, w), and ξ_{y'}(w) is a unit orientation of Q'.
  By step 1 both carriers equal tangentSpace(M, w), so Q = Q' (a submodule is determined by its carrier). By orientation_sign, ξ_{y'}(w) = ξ_y(w) or ξ_{y'}(w) = −ξ_y(w). Assume the latter; we derive a contradiction.
 (b) Let L be given by unit_orientation_dual, and put β := L(ξ_y(w)). Part (c) of that lemma gives ξ_y(w)(β) = 1, hence ξ_{y'}(w)(β) = −1.
 (c) Put f(x) := ξ_y(x)(β) and g(x) := ξ_{y'}(x)(β).
  - Orientations are continuous on their sets, and evaluation at β is continuous. So f is continuous on M ∩ B_y and g on M ∩ B_{y'}.
  - Both sets are neighbourhoods of w relative to M, and f(w) = 1, g(w) = −1.
  - B_y ∩ B_{y'} is an open set containing w.
  Hence there is r > 0 with B_r(w) ⊆ B_y ∩ B_{y'} such that f(x) > 1/2 and g(x) < −1/2 for every x ∈ M ∩ B_r(w).
 (d) Let φ : ℝ^P → [0, 1] be the smooth bump ContDiffBump centred at w with inner radius r/4 and outer radius r/2.
  - φ = 1 on closedBall(w, r/4), and tsupport φ = closedBall(w, r/2) ⊆ B_r(w) is compact.
  - For a covector γ put ω_γ(x) := φ(x)γ. It is smooth with compact support, so ω_γ ∈ 𝒟^m(ℝ^P), and tsupport ω_γ ⊆ B_r(w).
  - ω_{−β} = −ω_β.
 (e) Claim. Let z ∈ M with B_r(w) ⊆ B_z, and let γ be a covector with ξ_z(x)(γ) ≥ 1/2 for all x ∈ M ∩ B_r(w). Then C(ω_γ) > 0.
  Proof. tsupport ω_γ ⊆ B_z, so by hypothesis C(ω_γ) = ∫_{M ∩ B_z} F dH^m, where F(x) := ξ_z(x)(φ(x)γ) = φ(x)·ξ_z(x)(γ).
  - F is integrable on M ∩ B_z. It is continuous on the Borel set M ∩ B_z, hence a.e. strongly measurable for H^m restricted to it. Also |F(x)| ≤ |ξ_z(x)(γ)| ≤ |γ| by unit_orientation_dual (a), since ξ_z(x) is a unit orientation of a subspace. And H^m(M ∩ B_z) < ∞.

1. (6a: compact sets avoiding 0.) Let K be compact with 0 ∉ K.

2. (6b: closed balls about 0.) Let R > 0 and A := {x : R/2 ≤ |x| ≤ R}. A is closed and bounded, hence compact, and 0 ∉ A. By step 1, a := H^m(M ∩ A) < ∞.

 - Hence M ∩ closedBall(0, R) ⊆ ⋃_{k≥0} 2^{−k}·(M ∩ A).

  H^m(M ∩ closedBall(0, R)) ≤ Σ_{k≥0} H^m(2^{−k}·(M ∩ A)) = Σ_{k≥0} (2^{−m})^k·a = a·(1 − 2^{−m})⁻¹,
  a geometric series in [0, ∞].
 - This is finite, because 2^{−m} < 1 (m ≥ 1) and a < ∞.
3. (6c: arbitrary compact sets.) A compact K is bounded, so K ⊆ closedBall(0, R) for some R > 0 (any R ≥ 1 large enough). Then H^m(M ∩ K) ≤ H^m(M ∩ closedBall(0, R)) < ∞ by step 2. ∎

Here every point of O is assumed to have a neighbourhood with the local identity. In the parent, a point off spt C has the neighbourhood ℝ^P ∖ spt C, on which both sides vanish.
Notation: H^m := μHE[m], ⟨α, η⟩ := η(α), and |α| := covectorEuclideanNorm α.

1. (Finite cover.) K := tsupport ω is compact, as ω is a test form, and K ⊆ O. For each x ∈ K choose an open B_x ∋ x as in the hypothesis. Finitely many B_{x_1}, …, B_{x_N} cover K.
2. (Partition of unity.) Take a smooth partition of unity on ℝ^P on the closed set K, subordinate to this cover (Mathlib SmoothPartitionOfUnity.exists_isSubordinate with model ℝ^P). It gives smooth ψ_1, …, ψ_N : ℝ^P → ℝ with tsupport ψ_j ⊆ B_{x_j} and Σ_j ψ_j = 1 on K.
3. (The pieces.) For each j put ω_j := ψ_jω.
 - ω_j is smooth, and tsupport ω_j ⊆ tsupport ψ_j ∩ tsupport ω ⊆ B_{x_j} ∩ K.
 - So tsupport ω_j is compact (a closed subset of K), and ω_j ∈ 𝒟^m(ℝ^P).
 - The hypothesis for B_{x_j} gives C(ω_j) = ∫_M ⟨ψ_jω, ξ⟩ dH^m.
4. (Splitting ω.) ω = Σ_j ω_j pointwise. On K, Σ_j ψ_j(x)ω(x) = ω(x). Off K, ω(x) = 0 and every term vanishes. By linearity of C, C(ω) = Σ_j C(ω_j).
5. (Integrability.) Each F_j(x) := ⟨ψ_j(x)ω(x), ξ(x)⟩ is integrable on M.
 - F_j is continuous on the Borel set M, hence a.e. strongly measurable for H^m⌞M. Here ξ is continuous on M, ψ_jω is continuous, and evaluation is continuous.
 - x ↦ |ψ_j(x)ω(x)| is continuous with compact support, so it is bounded by some S_j. Here |·| = covectorEuclideanNorm is continuous: it is the square root of a finite sum of squares of the continuous evaluations α ↦ α(e_{I(0)}, …, e_{I(m−1)}), and it vanishes at 0.
 - For x ∈ M ∩ K, |F_j(x)| ≤ |ψ_j(x)ω(x)| ≤ S_j, by the hypothesis |⟨α, ξ(x)⟩| ≤ |α|. For x ∈ M ∖ K, ω(x) = 0, so F_j(x) = 0.
 - S_j·1_K is integrable for H^m⌞M, because H^m(M ∩ K) < ∞.
6. (Summation.) C(ω) = Σ_j ∫_M F_j dH^m = ∫_M Σ_j F_j dH^m = ∫_M ⟨Σ_j ψ_jω, ξ⟩ dH^m = ∫_M ⟨ω, ξ⟩ dH^m. This uses linearity of the integral for integrable functions, linearity of each ξ(x), and step 4. ∎

Source. Step 8 of the supplied parent proof (parent B0.1). There it is applied to χ_εω; here it is stated for any sequence of test forms that concentrate at 0 with bounded coefficients. Book: Simon Ch. 6, 3.1 (integer multiplicity currents).
Notation: H^m := μHE[m], and |α| := covectorEuclideanNorm α.

1. (Representation.) C is integer multiplicity, so fix an IMRep R = (M_R, θ_R, ξ_R) with R.Represents C. For every k,
 C(ω_k) = ∫_{M_R} θ_R(x)·ξ_R(x)(ω_k(x)) dH^m(x) =: ∫_{M_R} F_k dH^m.
2. (A fixed ball.) A convergent real sequence is bounded, so fix R₀ with r_k ≤ R₀ for all k. Then ω_k(x) = 0 whenever |x| > R₀, since |x| > R₀ ≥ r_k.
3. (Domination.) By R.orients, for H^m-a.e. x ∈ M_R, ξ_R(x) is a unit orientation of a subspace. For such x, unit_orientation_dual (a) gives |ξ_R(x)(α)| ≤ |α| for every covector α. Then:
 - if |x| ≤ R₀, |F_k(x)| ≤ θ_R(x)·|ω_k(x)| ≤ c·θ_R(x);
 - if |x| > R₀, F_k(x) = 0.
 So |F_k| ≤ G := c·θ_R·1_{closedBall(0, R₀)} a.e. on M_R, for every k.
4. (Integrability and measurability.)
 - G is integrable on M_R: θ_R is measurable, and ∫_{M_R ∩ closedBall(0,R₀)} θ_R dH^m < ∞ by R.locallyIntegrable_mult with the compact K = closedBall(0, R₀) ⊆ ℝ^P.
 - Each F_k is a.e. strongly measurable on M_R: θ_R is measurable, ξ_R is a.e. strongly measurable for H^m⌞M_R, ω_k is continuous, and (η, α) ↦ η(α) is continuous.
5. (Pointwise limit.) Let x ≠ 0. Since r_k → 0 < |x|, we have r_k < |x| for all large k, so ω_k(x) = 0 and F_k(x) = 0 eventually. Moreover H^m({0}) = 0 because m ≥ 1: μHE[m] is a multiple of μH[m], which has no atoms in positive dimension (Measure.nullSingletonClass_hausdorff). Hence F_k → 0 a.e. on M_R.
6. By dominated convergence, C(ω_k) = ∫ F_k → ∫ 0 = 0. ∎

Notation: H^m := μHE[m], ⟨α, η⟩ := η(α), and |α| := covectorEuclideanNorm α.
Fix ω ∈ 𝒟^m(ℝ^P) and put K := tsupport ω, a compact set.

1. (Bounds.)
 - |·| is continuous: it is the square root of a finite sum of squares of the continuous evaluations α ↦ α(e_{I(0)}, …, e_{I(m−1)}).
 - |·| is absolutely homogeneous: |aα| = |a|·|α|, because each evaluation scales by a.
 - x ↦ |ω(x)| is continuous with compact support, so |ω(x)| ≤ S for some S and all x.
2. (Cut-offs.) For k ∈ ℕ let ε_k := 1/(k+1), and let χ_k : ℝ^P → [0, 1] be the smooth bump ContDiffBump centred at 0 with radii ε_k < 2ε_k. Then χ_k = 1 on closedBall(0, ε_k) and support χ_k = B_{2ε_k}(0).
 - ω_k^in := χ_kω and ω_k^out := (1 − χ_k)ω are smooth with support in K, so they lie in 𝒟^m(ℝ^P).
 - ω = ω_k^in + ω_k^out, so C(ω) = C(ω_k^in) + C(ω_k^out) by linearity.
3. (Step 8: C(ω_k^in) → 0.) Apply vertex_negligible with r_k := 2ε_k → 0 and c := S.
 - If |x| ≥ 2ε_k then χ_k(x) = 0, so ω_k^in(x) = 0.
 - |ω_k^in(x)| = χ_k(x)·|ω(x)| ≤ S.
 Hence C(ω_k^in) → 0.
4. (The outer parts.) (1 − χ_k)ω vanishes on the open ball B_{ε_k}(0) ∋ 0, so 0 ∉ tsupport ω_k^out. By hypothesis,
 C(ω_k^out) = ∫_M ⟨(1 − χ_k)ω, ξ⟩ dH^m = ∫_M (1 − χ_k(x))·ξ(x)(ω(x)) dH^m(x) =: ∫_M G_k dH^m.
5. (Step 9: dominated convergence on M.)
 - G_k is continuous on the Borel set M, hence a.e. strongly measurable for H^m⌞M.
 - For x ∈ M ∩ K, |G_k(x)| ≤ |1 − χ_k(x)|·|ξ(x)(ω(x))| ≤ |ω(x)| ≤ S, using 0 ≤ χ_k ≤ 1 and the hypothesis on ξ. For x ∈ M ∖ K, ω(x) = 0, so G_k(x) = 0.
 - So |G_k| ≤ S·1_K on M. This bound is integrable for H^m⌞M because H^m(M ∩ K) < ∞.
 - For x ∈ M we have x ≠ 0 (0 ∉ M). Once 2ε_k < |x|, χ_k(x) = 0 and G_k(x) = ξ(x)(ω(x)).
 Hence ∫_M G_k dH^m → ∫_M ⟨ω, ξ⟩ dH^m.
6. Therefore C(ω) = C(ω_k^in) + C(ω_k^out) → 0 + ∫_M ⟨ω, ξ⟩ dH^m. The left side does not depend on k, so by uniqueness of limits C(ω) = ∫_M ⟨ω(x), ξ(x)⟩ dH^m(x). ∎
